description:
OrbitXI is a multidisciplinary team passionate about space exploration, artificial intelligence, and data-driven innovation. We aim to combine AI, machine learning, software engineering, and creative problem-solving to address real-world challenges using NASA’s open data.

We welcome motivated developers, designers, data scientists, and space enthusiasts to collaborate, learn, and build impactful solutions.
summary: Lunar Landing Site Navigator is a web tool that compares two places on the Moon over the same dates. For each site it shows how high the Sun and the Earth are above the local horizon, and when each is above it, using position data from the NASA/JPL Horizons System. Sunlight and a line of sight to Earth are two of the first questions asked about any lunar surface location, and they change with both place and time. The tool puts two sites side by side in an answer-first summary, a visibility timeline, a sky view, shared charts and a visibility table, labels every data series with its source and retrieval time, and states its limits plainly: results are sampled geometric estimates over a smooth sphere with site height assumed to be 0 km. Terrain, solar-power output and radio-link quality are not modelled; a 3D Moon and terrain views built from NASA LRO data show where the sites are, for context only. It is a first-look comparison and teaching tool, not a landing-site selection or mission-planning system.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

The user picks two sites on the Moon (a preset or custom latitude, east longitude and height), a start date, a number of days (up to 62) and a sampling interval (10 minutes to 1 day). The app requests Sun and Earth positions for both sites from the NASA/JPL Horizons System and shows:

- Sun elevation and Earth elevation above the local horizon for both sites on shared charts (Site A solid, Site B dashed), with the 0-degree horizon marked;

- a visibility table: number of samples with the Sun above the horizon, with the Earth above the horizon, and with both together; estimated durations; estimated first rise time;

- a comparison summary, shown first, stating which site has the longer estimated time above the horizon, and by how much, with the share of samples above the horizon and the longest estimated Sun window for each site;

- a visibility timeline (bars for when each body is above the 0-degree horizon at each site) and a sky view (Sun and Earth azimuth and elevation at a chosen time, read directly from the Horizons samples), linked to the charts by one time cursor with play and pause;

- context views that are NOT used in any calculation: a rotatable 3D Moon with the two sites pinned at the entered coordinates (NASA LRO LROC colour over LOLA elevation, relief exaggerated 6 times, as labelled) and a terrain close-up around each preset site from NASA LOLA elevation. Their lighting is illustrative, not a prediction of illumination;

- for every data series, its source label (LIVE, CACHED or ARCHIVED), retrieval time and a link to the exact NASA request.

HOW IT WORKS

A Next.js server route builds a Horizons API observer-table request for a surface site on the Moon (centre "coord@301", geodetic coordinates, quantity 4 = apparent azimuth and elevation, airless model). Each Horizons response reports the ephemeris (DE441) and the site frame (MEAN_ME, high precision); the app shows these. The visibility figures are calculated from the returned elevations by fixed rules in the project code: a body counts as above the horizon when the elevation of its centre is above 0 degrees. Rise and set times are estimated by straight-line interpolation between adjacent samples and are marked as estimates. No value shown is typed in by hand or produced by an AI model. The app's output was compared row by row with direct Horizons requests (721 rows per series, no differences) on the deployed build.

SITES OFFERED

- Six Apollo landing sites (coordinates from NASA NSSDCA), as historical validation examples. They are not lunar south-pole candidates.

- Two NASA 2023 regional reference points near the lunar south pole: Nobile Rim 1 and Malapert Massif (centre-point coordinates from NASA's Lunar Surface Data Book, ACD-50044 Rev A, 2023, Appendix A2, Table A2-2). These are NOT approved landing sites. They are reference points of regions in a 2023 NASA table; a region is far larger than a point.

- A technical verification point from the Horizons manual, and custom coordinates.

LIMITATIONS (also stated in the app)

- Angles are geometric, for the centre of the Sun or Earth, measured from the horizontal plane of a smooth sphere of radius 1737.4 km.

- Site height is assumed to be 0 km. Terrain is not included in any visibility result, although real terrain is displayed for context (the two south-pole reference points lie on high ground, which the calculation ignores): mountains and crater rims can hide the Sun or Earth even when the angle is positive, especially near the poles, where both stay within a few degrees of the horizon.

- Results are sampled estimates: an event shorter than the sampling interval can be missed, and counts depend on the interval chosen.

- This is not a solar-power or temperature estimate, and the Earth being above the horizon does not guarantee a working communication link. It is not a landing-site safety assessment.

- Near the poles, small differences in coordinate frame or longitude convention can change whether a sample counts as visible. The team's science review accepted the south-pole reference points for approximate regional geometric comparison only.

WHY IT MATTERS

A clear, honest first comparison of illumination and Earth-visibility geometry helps students and early-stage planners see why location and date both matter on the Moon, and what a geometric answer can and cannot tell them, before terrain-aware tools are used.

TOOLS

TypeScript, Next.js 16, React 19, Tailwind CSS 4, Recharts 3, three.js (3D context views), Vitest (169 automated tests), hosted on Vercel. Source code, tests, stored example responses, citations and known issues: https://github.com/dingchengzhu25-cmd/OrbitXI-Lunar-Landing-Site-Navigator-1

TESTING AND KNOWN ISSUES

The submitted build was tested by the developer (automated tests, browser checks on desktop and phone widths, comparison with direct Horizons output). The team's QA lead tested an earlier build; his findings on phone layout were fixed afterwards and retested by the developer, not independently. The user-interface redesign was made by the team's UX member and reviewed by the developer before release. Not tested: behaviour with WebGL turned off, very small phones and real devices. Known open issues are listed in the repository.

DEMO VIDEO

The 29-second video is made only of real screen captures of the live site (build 5ea3c50) comparing two NASA 2023 regional reference points, Nobile Rim 1 and Malapert Massif, for 30 days from 14 November 2026 UTC with hourly samples, with on-screen English text. It has no narration; the music is 'Aphelion' by Scott Buckley, released under CC BY 4.0 (https://www.scottbuckley.com.au/library/aphelion/), edited excerpt used in the demo. The Moon imagery and terrain visible in it are parts of the site itself and come from NASA LRO data, shown for context only. Not affiliated with or endorsed by NASA.

USE OF AI (SI) TOOLS

Code: the application's source code, tests and documentation were written with Claude Code (Anthropic) under the team lead's direction; this is acknowledged in the repository README and Claude is named as co-author in the commit history. Planning, coordination and source research used ChatGPT (OpenAI). Part of the QA used AI-assisted checks (Codex, OpenAI), recorded separately from personal testing. A design prototype, not part of the app, was built as a Claude artifact. Video: the demo video contains no AI-generated audio, images or video; it was assembled with Claude Code (script-driven screen captures of our live site and FFmpeg editing), and its on-screen text was drafted with AI and approved by the team lead. Data: the numbers the app shows are NASA/JPL Horizons output and deterministic calculations from it, not AI output. Some team members also used AI assistants for their own working documents; the tools used by two members are not recorded.
